stem: An adult client is prescribed IV palonosetron before moderately emetogenic cancer chemotherapy. Which outcome is consistent with the medication's FDA-labeled use in this setting?

options.A: Prevention of both acute and delayed chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting.
options.B: Treatment of nausea only after vomiting has already begun following chemotherapy.
options.C: Prevention of acute nausea only, with no labeled role in delayed nausea or vomiting.
options.D: Relief of chemotherapy-related pain rather than prevention of nausea and vomiting.

rationale: Palonosetron is a 5-HT3 receptor antagonist. In adults, its prescribing information includes prevention of both acute and delayed nausea and vomiting associated with initial and repeat courses of moderately emetogenic cancer chemotherapy. It is administered prophylactically before chemotherapy; it is not an analgesic and its labeled adult indication for moderately emetogenic chemotherapy is not limited to the acute phase.
educational_objective: Recognize the labeled role of IV palonosetron in adults for prevention of both acute and delayed nausea and vomiting associated with moderately emetogenic chemotherapy.
source_organization: DailyMed, U.S. National Library of Medicine

source_claim_supported: In adults, palonosetron hydrochloride injection is indicated for prevention of acute and delayed nausea and vomiting associated with initial and repeat courses of moderately emetogenic cancer chemotherapy and is given as a single IV dose beginning approximately 30 minutes before chemotherapy.

correction_summary: Rebuilt the original comparative half-life item into a direct label-based indication question. Removed the inference that pharmacokinetic half-life alone proves delayed antiemetic coverage, specified an adult receiving moderately emetogenic chemotherapy, used a current July 2026 DailyMed label, and rewrote distractors so only one option matches the FDA-labeled preventive role.
audit_findings: Original item inferred clinical delayed-emesis coverage from comparative half-life rather than anchoring the answer directly to the labeled indication.
The current July 6, 2026 DailyMed label directly supports prevention of acute and delayed CINV in adults receiving moderately emetogenic chemotherapy.
The rebuilt item avoids overgeneralizing the adult HEC indication, for which the label specifies prevention of acute nausea and vomiting.
Prophylactic timing is supported by the label and no treatment-after-onset claim is implied.
Independent adversarial review found no ambiguity, second valid answer, cueing, or unsupported precision.
